claims.text: Nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its simple solid-solution state.
The low hardness and strength are governed by the alloy's single-phase simple solid-solution state.
Nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the proposed initial state has relatively high stacking-fault energy.
The initial CoCrFeNiTi state lacks significant nanoprecipitates and dislocation networks.
The applicable initial material is a homogeneous, single-phase CoCrFeNiTi solid solution with low defect density.
Cold rolling followed by annealing can be used to induce nanoprecipitates or increase dislocation density in CoCrFeNiTi.
Fine nanoprecipitates and enhanced dislocation substructures obstruct dislocation glide.
High stacking-fault energy and an absence of microstructural barriers enable near-unimpeded dislocation glide in pristine CoCrFeNiTi.
Near-unimpeded dislocation glide produces high plasticity but low strain-hardening ability.
Introducing nanoscale obstacles increases the stress required for dislocation motion.
Microstructural obstacles can increase alloy strength and hardness through conventional strengthening mechanisms.
Thermomechanically processed CoCrFeNiTi will have higher yield strength than the starting simple solid solution.
Thermomechanically processed CoCrFeNiTi will have higher hardness than the starting simple solid solution.
Thermomechanically processed CoCrFeNiTi will exhibit enhanced work hardening because of increased dislocation interactions.
The strengthening treatment may slightly reduce ductility.
The initial alloy's favorable plasticity and machinability arise from its defect-sparse single-phase state.
The hypothesis is restricted to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi lacking preexisting precipitates or substantial dislocation tangles.
The proposed comparison uses room-temperature quasi-static tensile or compression loading.
